bibliographic.abstract: Decoherence remains a critical obstacle to achieving high-fidelity, scalable superconducting qubits, with the tunnel barrier of Josephson junctions a key source of loss. Here we apply resonant X-ray reflectivity to non-destructively probe the electronic structure of buried layers in Al/AlO_x/Al Josephson junctions. At the Al K-edge, energy-dependent modulations in the reflectivity maps enable Kramers–Kronig–constrained extraction of the layer-resolved atomic scattering factors. The analysis reveals that the barrier coordination evolves from more tetrahedral toward predominantly octahedral character with increasing oxidation pressure. At the interfaces, the lower metal–oxide boundary is comparatively under-coordinated and disordered relative to the upper interface. Comparison with simulated X-ray absorption spectra identifies the dominant coordination motifs within the oxide and its interfaces, providing depth-resolved structural insight that constrains microscopic models of two-level system formation. These results link growth conditions, local coordination environments, and junction electronic properties, demonstrating resonant X-ray reflectivity as a powerful tool for probing the microscopic materials properties of Josephson junctions and providing a materials-level framework for mitigating decoherence in superconducting qubits.

datasets.dataset_description: Energy-dependent reflectivity maps measured at the Al K-edge (1540 eV to 1590 eV) to extract layer-resolved atomic scattering factors and coordination environments.
Reflectivity scans collected at non-resonant photon energies of 1548 eV and 524 eV to determine the underlying layer structure.
Al K-edge XAS spectra acquired in total electron yield mode and converted to atomic scattering factors for resonant reflectivity modeling.
ELNES measurements at the Al L2,3 and O K edges to probe local coordination environments.
I-V measurements fitted to the Simmons tunneling model to extract barrier height and thickness.
